newsitem.title: USA: Clinton upbeat on U.N. debt, but GOP setting terms.
newsitem.headline: Clinton upbeat on U.N. debt, but GOP setting terms.

text.p: President Bill Clinton promised to pay off hefty U.S. debts to the United Nations on Thursday and in return Secretary-General Kofi Annan pledged that the world body would carry out wide-ranging reforms.

"As the United Nations moves to reform it must know also that the United States is prepared to pay its way," Clinton told reporters after a White House meeting with Annan, who took office on January 1, replacing Boutros Boutros-Ghali, who was opposed by the United States.
"In the weeks ahead I will be working with Congress to reach an agreement through which America can pay our arrears to the U.N., meet our obligations," Clinton said.

"Our budget will actually have a plan to pay it back, and to pay it back in a prompt fashion," he said in reference to his proposal to pay about $1 billion to the United Nations by 1999 providing wide-ranging reform is underway.
Annan, a 58-year old Ghanian, who was meeting some of the harshest U.N. critics in Congress during his three-day visit, emphasised that he too was committed to reform.
"If we don't change we may lose our relevance," the graying, soft-spoken veteran U.N. official said.

"Simply put, what the United Nations wants is what the U.S. also wants -- a reformed United Nations that is effective, efficient, leaner and relevant to the tasks that member states want to set for us," he said.

The United States legally owes the world body $1.3 billion, but the computation in Washington is $500 million less because of unilateral deductions by Congress over the years, especially since Republicans came to power in 1994.

Annan was backed strongly by the Clinton administration when he was elected to succeed Boutros-Ghali, who had been villified by conservatives in Congress for his independence and as a block to fundamental reforms.
Annan also made some headway in a meeting with more than a dozen members of the Senator Foreign Relations Committee, headed by Senator Jesse Helms, a longtime foe of the United Nations.

In a statement welcoming Annan, Helms told him that if his reforms were piecemeal "you will have a very difficult time convincing Congress to send more American tax dollars to the U.N. "So, Mr Annan, the ball is in your court."
Helms said he planned to introduce legislation setting benchmarks -- or conditions-- for reform before any funds could be paid.
U.N. officials said Annan and Helms agreed to have their staffs meet soon to discuss legislation the committee was drawing up.

But despite the cooperation, unilateral conditions imposed on 185 member states belonging to the United Nations may meet tough resistance, particularly the European Union countries and Japan who pay for most of the world body.
Most Republican leaders have expressed a willingness to pay off the debt but several have attached conditions that appear beyond the power of any U.N. chief to deliver.

New York Republican Benjamin Gilman, chairman of the House International Relations Committee, told Annan on Wednesday U.S. dues should be cut from 25 percent to 20 percent of the U.N. regular budget, which is calculated by members' wealth.
Annan, however, in comments earlier in the day warned that reform could not be accomplished on a "shoestring budget".
Annan said he sensed a "new beginning" in relations with Washington. He said it was symbolic that he was Clinton's first prominent visitor since the president's second-term inauguration on Monday.
